Continuation round 1 covered only Chapter 1B. No score or score range was assigned.

Because the filesystem is read-only, I could not update the supplied `research-materials.md` or `research-ledger-manifest.json`. The complete append-only handoff and manifest entries are below; parent persistence is required.

## New evidence register entries

All new IDs continue after E020.

### E021 — IAEA regulatory-independence weakness

- Canonical fact key: `https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/documents/review-missions/final_irrs_report_bangladesh.pdf#PDF-p17-18-regulatory-independence`
- Source: *Final Report of the Integrated Regulatory Review Service Mission to Bangladesh*, IAEA, mission completed December 2022; report publication date later.
- Locator: PDF pp. 17–18, sections on governmental responsibilities and BAERA independence.
- Claim: The IAEA identified a potential future compromise of BAERA’s independence because the ministry responsible for delivering the nuclear power programme also had responsibilities relevant to regulation. It issued a recommendation that Bangladesh ensure BAERA can make safety decisions independently.
- Role: Adverse, target-period regulatory-risk evidence.
- Source type/confidence: Intergovernmental independent assessment; high. It directly assessed Bangladesh’s regulatory framework during the 2022 mission.
- Attribution: Formal government/system responsibility; does not establish Sheikh Hasina’s personal direction or operational negligence.
- Lens mapping: `1B.4`, `1B.6`, `1B.9`, `1B.10`.
- Contrary/limitation: The same mission recognized functioning regulatory structures and ongoing oversight; this is a governance vulnerability, not a finding of unsafe operation.
- URL: [IAEA final IRRS report](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/documents/review-missions/final_irrs_report_bangladesh.pdf)

### E022 — Inspector retention and incomplete regulatory procedures

- Canonical fact key: `https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/documents/review-missions/final_irrs_report_bangladesh.pdf#PDF-p32-33-inspector-retention-procedures`
- Source: Same IAEA IRRS report.
- Locator: PDF pp. 32–33, sections concerning Rooppur inspection, resident inspectors, staffing, and regulatory procedures.
- Claim: BAERA had a resident inspector and inspection arrangements at Rooppur, but the mission recorded inspector-retention problems, limited continuity of experience, and procedures or management documentation still under development.
- Role: Mixed, with adverse operational-capacity implications and positive evidence of actual inspection presence.
- Source type/confidence: Intergovernmental independent assessment; high.
- Attribution: Institutional and ministerial capacity; no evidence of a Hasina order, concealment, or personal command practice.
- Lens mapping: `1B.5`, `1B.6`, `1B.9`, `1B.10`.
- Contrary/limitation: The report also records announced and unannounced inspections and a resident inspector; the evidence does not establish a safety incident or catastrophic-risk failure.
- URL: [IAEA final IRRS report](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/documents/review-missions/final_irrs_report_bangladesh.pdf)

### E023 — Formal 2022 Rooppur licensing and oversight architecture

- Canonical fact key: `https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/24/02/cns_bangladesh_national_report_2022.pdf#PDF-p7-12-BAERA-Rooppur-licensing`
- Source: *Bangladesh National Report to the Ninth Review Meeting of the Convention on Nuclear Safety*, Government of Bangladesh/IAEA, 2022.
- Locator: PDF pp. 7–12, sections on BAERA, government committees, licensing, PSAR review, and Rooppur construction.
- Claim: Bangladesh reported that BAERA had statutory authority to regulate nuclear safety; BAERA reviewed the preliminary safety analysis and soil-stabilization safety material before issuing siting/design/construction licences; Rooppur was still under construction and no nuclear power unit was operational in the target year.
- Role: Positive formal/contextual evidence; target-year end-posture evidence.
- Source type/confidence: Official national report submitted under an international nuclear-safety convention; medium-high for laws, licenses, and project status; lower for self-reported effectiveness.
- Attribution: Formal executive and regulatory responsibility; does not establish personal performance by Hasina.
- Lens mapping: `1B.1`, `1B.4`, `1B.6`, `1B.8`, `1B.10`.
- Contrary/limitation: The report is a government submission and its claims of progress require independent corroboration. The IAEA IRRS findings in E021–E022 qualify the formal architecture.
- URL: [Bangladesh National Report 2022](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/24/02/cns_bangladesh_national_report_2022.pdf)

### E024 — Contemporary independent account of the 2022 IRRS mission

- Canonical fact key: `https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/articles/iaea-says-bangladesh-committed-to-nuclear-safety#2022-12-15-IRRS`
- Source: “IAEA says Bangladesh committed to nuclear safety,” World Nuclear News, 15 December 2022.
- Locator: Article paragraphs describing the 13-day mission ending 8 December 2022 and the mission’s purpose and findings.
- Claim: The IAEA’s first IRRS mission to Bangladesh assessed the national nuclear/radiation safety regulatory framework at the government’s request and identified areas for improvement while describing a commitment to continuous safety improvement.
- Role: Mixed corroboration of E021–E023; not an independent operational safety audit itself.
- Source type/confidence: Specialist nuclear-industry reporting reproducing the mission’s contemporary public account; medium-high.
- Attribution: Government-requested institutional review; no personal Hasina attribution.
- Lens mapping: `1B.4`, `1B.6`, `1B.10`.
- Contrary/limitation: It should not be treated as evidence that Rooppur was operationally safe or that Hasina personally ensured safety.
- URL: [World Nuclear News report](https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/articles/iaea-says-bangladesh-committed-to-nuclear-safety)

### E025 — 2022 anti-nuclear-weapons rhetoric

- Canonical fact key: `https://nypm.mofa.gov.bd/pages/static-pages/6952667535ce18e1c05a941c#2022-10-17-nuclear-weapons-statement`
- Source: “2022 Statement: Thematic Debate—Nuclear Weapons,” Permanent Mission of Bangladesh to the UN, 17 October 2022.
- Candidate status: `discovery_only`, not counted as defensible evidence.
- Reason: The underlying page repeatedly failed to fetch. Search output exposed the statement’s text, but the source was not independently opened or verified at locator level.
- Potential use if later authenticated: Bangladesh’s representative described nuclear weapons as an unacceptable threat and supported elimination and negative-security assurances.
- Attribution limit: This is a foreign-ministry/UN-representative statement, not necessarily a personal statement by Hasina and not evidence of crisis conduct.
- Potential lens mapping: `1B.2`, `1B.3`, `1B.7`.

### E026 — Bangladesh’s formal non-nuclear safeguards status

- Canonical fact key: `https://ola.iaea.org/Applications/FactSheets/Country/Detail?code=BD#NPT-safeguards`
- Source: IAEA Office of Legal Affairs, Bangladesh country treaty factsheet.
- Locator: Entries for the NPT safeguards agreement dated 11 June 1982 and Additional Protocol dated 30 March 2001.
- Claim: Bangladesh has an NPT safeguards agreement and an Additional Protocol with the IAEA.
- Role: Contextual inherited and target-period nonproliferation baseline.
- Source type/confidence: Intergovernmental treaty record; high for treaty status.
- Attribution: State-level legal commitment; no personal attribution.
- Lens mapping: `1B.1`, `1B.4`, `1B.7`, `1B.10`.
- Contrary/limitation: Treaty status does not establish complete compliance, command practice, or ruler-specific risk reduction.
- URL: [IAEA Bangladesh treaty factsheet](https://ola.iaea.org/Applications/FactSheets/Country/Detail?code=BD)

### E027 — 2022 critical-information-infrastructure designation

- Canonical fact key: `https://www.dpp.gov.bd/bgpress/index.php/document/get_extraordinary/46206#2022-10-02-CII-gazette`
- Source: Bangladesh Government Press, Extraordinary Gazette, 2 October 2022.
- Locator: Gazette listing at lines/pages 15919–15920; entry dated 2 October 2022.
- Claim: Bangladesh formally designated 29 institutions as critical information infrastructure under the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology.
- Role: Positive formal cyber-governance evidence, but not nuclear-specific.
- Source type/confidence: Official gazette record; high for the designation.
- Attribution: Formal government action during Hasina’s tenure; personal authorship or operational implementation is not established.
- Lens mapping: `1B.9`.
- Contrary/limitation: The record does not show whether Rooppur was included, whether audits occurred, or whether the controls reduced catastrophic cyber risk.
- URL: [Bangladesh Government Press gazette record](https://www.dpp.gov.bd/bgpress/index.php/document/get_extraordinary/46206)

### E028 — Independent 2022 cyber-capacity profile

- Canonical fact key: `https://ncsi.ega.ee/country/bd_2022/?allData=1#CII-monitoring`
- Source: National Cyber Security Index, Bangladesh 2022 country profile, e-Governance Academy.
- Locator: Sections 1.3, 6.1–6.4; especially the discussion of critical-information-infrastructure inspection reporting.
- Claim: The 2022 profile records formal cyber-security strategy and CII oversight mechanisms, including a legal requirement for annual inspection reporting, while also showing gaps in implementation-plan and supervisory-capacity indicators.
- Role: Mixed independent contextual evidence.
- Source type/confidence: Comparative external assessment using official legal sources; medium-high.
- Attribution: State institutional capacity; no personal Hasina nexus.
- Lens mapping: `1B.9`.
- Contrary/limitation: It is a national cyber-capacity profile, not an assessment of nuclear-plant cyber controls, dual-use targeting, or AI-enabled catastrophic pathways.
- URL: [NCSI Bangladesh 2022 profile](https://ncsi.ega.ee/country/bd_2022/?allData=1)

### E029 — Critical-infrastructure cyber guidelines recorded by the IEA

- Canonical fact key: `https://www.iea.org/policies/26644-digital-security-protection-guidelines-for-critical-information-infrastructure-2022#policy`
- Source: International Energy Agency policy database, “Digital Security Protection Guidelines for Critical Information Infrastructure 2022.”
- Locator: Country Bangladesh; year 2022; policy description.
- Claim: Bangladesh adopted 2022 guidelines intended to protect critical digital assets, including energy-sector operators.
- Role: Contextual corroboration of E027–E028.
- Source type/confidence: International policy database; medium.
- Attribution: Government policy record; effectiveness and personal decision nexus unknown.
- Lens mapping: `1B.9`.
- Contrary/limitation: No Rooppur-specific cyber assessment or evidence of implementation was located.
- URL: [IEA policy record](https://www.iea.org/policies/26644-digital-security-protection-guidelines-for-critical-information-infrastructure-2022)

### E030 — AI strategy and explicit recognition of AI-safety gaps

- Canonical fact key: `https://www.bangladeshtradeportal.gov.bd/kcfinder/upload/files/National_Strategy_for_Artificial_Intellgence_-_Bangladesh_.pdf#PDF-p47-AI-safety`
- Source: *National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence—Bangladesh*, Government of Bangladesh/ICT Division, 2020.
- Locator: PDF pp. 2–3, 46–49; sections on ethics, data privacy, security, regulations, accountability, AI safety, and legal/ethical frameworks.
- Claim: Bangladesh’s strategy identified AI ethics, data privacy, security, accountability, transparency, AI safety, and legal/ethical frameworks as policy needs; it also described limited technological adoption and infrastructure as challenges.
- Role: Inherited programme/context evidence for the dual-use governance gap.
- Source type/confidence: Official strategy document; high for stated policy intent, low for 2022 implementation.
- Attribution: Government strategy during Hasina’s tenure; no evidence of personal authorship or implementation in 2022.
- Lens mapping: `1B.9`.
- Contrary/limitation: The document is from 2020 and contains plans rather than target-year implementation or catastrophic-risk controls.
- URL: [Bangladesh National AI Strategy](https://www.bangladeshtradeportal.gov.bd/kcfinder/upload/files/National_Strategy_for_Artificial_Intellgence_-_Bangladesh_.pdf)

### E031 — Existing biosafety framework, without target-year operational proof

- Canonical fact key: `https://bangladeshbiosafety.org/bangladesh-documents/biosafety-regulatory-documents/#2008-2012-framework`
- Source: Bangladesh Biosafety Portal, regulatory-document index.
- Locator: Entries for the 2007/2008 Biosafety Guidelines, 2012 Bangladesh Biosafety Rules, and 2018 GMO emergency-response procedures.
- Claim: Bangladesh had a formal biosafety framework predating 2022, including rules for genetically engineered products and emergency procedures for contained research, field trials, transport, import, export, and transit.
- Role: Inherited-capacity context.
- Source type/confidence: Specialist biosafety document repository; medium.
- Attribution: State regulatory framework; no evidence of Hasina’s personal direction or target-year performance.
- Lens mapping: `1B.9`.
- Contrary/limitation: The portal lists no 2022 operational safety audit, dual-use review, or biological-risk incident assessment. The 2024 biosafety policy was excluded as post-period.
- URL: [Bangladesh Biosafety regulatory documents](https://bangladeshbiosafety.org/bangladesh-documents/biosafety-regulatory-documents/)

## Candidate outcomes and rejected leads

- Bangladesh’s 2022 Myanmar-border shelling and statements that Bangladesh wanted a peaceful solution and would use the UN were opened in *The Business Standard* and *The Daily Star*. They are useful for Chapter 2B, but were not retained for 1B because no nuclear, biological, AI, or other catastrophic-risk nexus was established. The sources are [TBS](https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/myanmar-border-shelling-issue-be-raised-un-if-necessary-says-kamal-497934) and [The Daily Star/Asia News Network](https://asianews.network/bangladesh-has-shown-patience-in-violation-of-land-and-airspace-by-myanmar-foreign-minister/).
- UN reporting on Myanmar airstrikes was rejected for 1B because it concerns Myanmar’s internal conflict and provides no Bangladesh catastrophic-risk attribution: [UN Myanmar statement](https://myanmar.un.org/en/204444-statement-united-nations-myanmar-reported-airstrikes-hpakant-kachin-state).
- The Bangladesh foreign-ministry nuclear statement was retained only as discovery material because the page could not be fetched reliably.
- BWC-specific country implementation material was found through the UNODA/UNIDIR-linked database, but the country page did not yield a stable opened locator in this run. It remains a discovery lead, not defensible evidence.
- Freedom House reporting on surveillance/interceptor purchases was not mapped to 1B: it concerns political surveillance, not a demonstrated catastrophic-risk pathway.
- No source established a Bangladesh nuclear command-and-control system, operational nuclear arsenal, nuclear crisis decision, biological-weapons programme, Rooppur-specific cyber assessment, or target-year cyber/AI incident.

## Chapter 1B yield and saturation assessment

The chapter now has:

- Existing evidence: E001–E003.
- New defensible source-claim units: E021–E024 and E026–E031.
- New discovery-only or rejected candidates: E025 and the Myanmar-border/UN leads.
- Independent source families represented: IAEA, Bangladesh Government Press, Bangladesh national report, IEA, NCSI/e-Governance Academy, Bangladesh Biosafety Portal, and specialist nuclear reporting.
- Same-URL split: the IAEA IRRS report is intentionally split into E021 and E022 because regulatory independence and inspector/procedure capacity are materially distinct claims.
- Cross-chapter reuse: E026–E031 are primarily Chapter 1B evidence; they should not be reused as proof of political freedom, integrity, or general effectiveness without separate attribution analysis.

The strongest improvement is the independent IAEA assessment of Rooppur’s regulatory and inspector-capacity vulnerabilities. The target-year end-posture is also clearer: Bangladesh remained a non-nuclear-weapon NPT state with Rooppur under construction rather than an operating nuclear power plant.

The following gaps remain genuinely unresolved after separate source-family searches:

- no ruler-specific nuclear crisis decision or threat episode;
- no operational nuclear command-and-control evidence;
- no independent Rooppur cyber-security assessment;
- no target-year implementation audit for Bangladesh’s AI or biosafety frameworks;
- no independent finding connecting Sheikh Hasina personally to nuclear-risk reduction or safety failures.

These gaps cannot be treated as evidence of safety or failure. They remain high-risk information-environment and attribution limitations.
